primary_text_note: 'Odour of Chrysanthemums' verified line by line against Project Gutenberg 22480; 'A Family Supper' verified against a full-text PDF; the five in-copyright stories verified by web search against study guides and quotation sets; exam claims verified against the AQA 8702 spec and the 8702/2 specimen paper.

findings.claim: "The central image is a pond in the garden"; the pond as a world "from which his mother is initially absent".
findings.truth: The pond is in the local public park and the mother is there too. Swift's opening: "The pond in our park was circular, exposed, perhaps fifty yards across."
findings.evidence: Story text quoted at american-scholars2017.blogspot.com and revisionworld.com/gcse-revision/english/short-stories/chemistry-graham-swift

findings.claim: "The story's emotional movement is driven by two losses: the grandmother's death ... and the arrival of Ralph." The lesson never mentions the narrator's dead father, the garden shed or the chemistry that names the story.
findings.truth: The narrator's father is dead (his plane went down in the Irish Sea) and mother and son have moved into the grandfather's house. The grandfather does chemical experiments in his garden shed and dies by drinking prussic acid taken from it. The shed and the chemistry are the story's title.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com Chemistry analysis; revisionworld.com; blog text quoting 'Laurel water. Prussic acid. Not for drinking.'

findings.claim: "His suicide by poisoning is never stated explicitly ... confirmed only through inference."
findings.truth: The story records a verdict of suicide by swallowing prussic acid. What is left uncertain is the narrator's suspicion that his mother drove the old man to it.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com Chemistry analysis: 'The official verdict is suicide, though the boy blames his mother.'

findings.claim: "Ralph is not a villain ... He is kind, tries to include the grandfather."
findings.truth: Ralph is a physically large, loud, coarse man whom the boy fears and hates. He displaces the grandfather to the shed, and the narrator plans to throw acid in his face.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com: 'a physically large man whom the boy fears and hates'; revisionworld: 'loud', 'coarse', narrator plans to 'throw acid in Ralph's face'.

findings.claim: "When the grandfather stops going to the pond ..."; "As Ralph's presence grows, the grandfather's visits to the pond become less frequent."
findings.truth: The outings end because the motor launch sinks; the narrator later believes his mother caused it. The grandfather then withdraws into his shed.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com: 'The boat eventually sinks, which the boy later believes his mother deliberately sabotaged.'

findings.claim: "His father was a coalmiiner"
findings.truth: Spelling: coalminer.
findings.evidence: typo in live copy

findings.claim: Walter "suffocated when a section of the mine shaft collapsed and trapped him underground".
findings.truth: The fall came down behind him at the coal face and shut him in without touching him. Gutenberg text: "it fell at th' back of 'im. 'E wor under th' face, an' it niver touched 'im. It shut 'im in. It seems 'e wor smothered."
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg 22480, The Prussian Officer and Other Stories, 'Odour of Chrysanthemums'

findings.claim: The chrysanthemums recall "her wedding, the births of her children, and moments of illness"; "Elizabeth's daughter brings a sprig into the house".
findings.truth: Elizabeth breaks off the twig herself and pushes it into her apron-band. Her three associations are her marriage, Annie's birth, and Walter's first drunkenness: "It was chrysanthemums when I married him, and chrysanthemums when you were born, and the first time they ever brought him home drunk, he'd got brown chrysanthemums in his button-hole." 'Moments of illness' is invented.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg 22480, story text

findings.claim: "A pen-pal scheme run by the school pairs British and Polish teachers; Carla signs up and is paired with Steve, a Polish-heritage teacher."
findings.truth: Carla is not a teacher and is not paired by a scheme. She overhears the head say Polish teachers want pen-friends in English schools, asks for an address, and writes to Stefan Jeziorny, a teacher in Poland. She hides her job and he assumes she is a teacher.
findings.evidence: studygroom.com; studienett.no/my-polish-teachers-tie/summary; shalom-education.com

findings.claim: The lesson's whole climax: Stefan "does not recognise Carla as his pen-friend because he sees only a canteen worker"; "the encounter is humiliating".
findings.truth: This does not happen. After Valerie and other staff mock Stefan's accent and tie, Carla goes up to him in her overall. He knows her at once, takes her hand and sings a Polish song from her childhood, and she sings with him. The ending is acceptance, not humiliation.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com: 'Stefan sings a Polish song from her childhood ... they sing together'; studygroom.com: 'He held his hand and sang a polish song'

findings.claim: "Steve ... his status as a teacher makes him part of the institution that categorises Carla as invisible ... not malicious, merely unthinking."
findings.truth: Stefan is the outsider the English staff look down on. Valerie mocks his accent and his ties. He is the one character who judges nobody by job, dress or accent.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com character notes on Stefan and Valerie

findings.claim: "the tie with its bright Polish colours".
findings.truth: The tie is "wider than normal ties, and it was red with bold green squiggles ... a terribly hopeful tie"; Carla calls it "a flag from another country, a better country". Red and green are not the Polish national colours.
findings.evidence: quoted story lines collated in GCSE quotation sets (quizlet, getrevising) for 'My Polish Teacher's Tie'

findings.claim: "The father recounts this story to his son ... The story is structured around the gradual, sickening accretion of evidence." The payout is repeatedly called insurance.
findings.truth: The narrator overhears one conversation between his father and a friend while waiting for his exam results. The dead boy is named Luke Moran; the American government paid the family a lump sum of $10,000 and $250 a month. It is state payment, not insurance. In the lavatory among the boxes of worms the narrator knows his 'youth had ended'; he then refuses to go.
findings.evidence: apersonalanthology.com/2023/06/30/korea-by-john-mcgahern; shalom-education.com Korea analysis

findings.claim: "a meal shadowed by poison, duty, and."
findings.truth: The description ends mid-sentence and is shown on the browse card.
findings.evidence: live field

findings.claim: "Watanabe's death is not condemned - it is described with a kind of reverence, as an act of principle"; "The father speaks of Watanabe's act with quiet approval". A knowledge check keys the answer "He admires death as an honourable response to shame and failure."
findings.truth: The father condemns it outright. Text: "'You think what he did - it was a mistake?' 'Why, of course. Do you see it otherwise?' ... 'There are other things besides work.'" He respects Watanabe the man ('a man of principle and honour') but not the act. The knowledge check therefore marked the true answer wrong.
findings.evidence: full story text, magicbarrel.wordpress.com PDF of 'A Family Supper'

findings.claim: "The mother's death from fugu is accidental."
findings.truth: The father says: "It's my belief that your mother's death was no accident. She had many worries. And some disappointments."
findings.evidence: full story text

findings.claim: "Ishiguro ... never shows the father preparing it."
findings.truth: The narrator and Kikuko find the father in the kitchen preparing the meal.
findings.evidence: full story text: 'We found my father in the kitchen.'

findings.claim: "the garden his mother tended appears uncared for"; "The garden, overgrown since the mother's death, symbolises what has been neglected."
findings.truth: No neglected garden appears in the story. The garden has thick foliage, a path through the shrubs and an old well. What signals loss is the house: rooms are 'startlingly empty' and the father says it is 'too large for a man to live in alone'.
findings.evidence: full story text

findings.claim: "the opening describes the narrator crossing Tokyo at night"; "the story stops before we see whether anyone rises from the table".
findings.truth: The story opens with a paragraph on how fugu kills, then the drive from the airport at the end of a sunny autumn day. The family finish the meal, get up, move to the tea-room and talk; the last line is 'We fell silent once more, waiting for Kikuko to bring the tea.'
findings.evidence: full story text

findings.claim: "injustice, voicelessness and dignity in a colonial Caribbean classroom".
findings.truth: Half the story takes place in England after the family emigrate, and it ends with the narrator being heard.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com 'Invisible Mass of the Back Row' analysis

findings.claim: "The narrator is unjustly punished - struck with a ruler by her teacher Miss Henderson for something she did not do. A more favoured child, sitting at the front, escapes justice while the narrator and others at the back are collectively blamed." The knowledge check keys this as the correct answer.
findings.truth: The narrator is Hortense. A school inspector asks about Columbus's arrival in the Caribbean; instead of the expected answer she asks what Columbus was doing there anyway, and Miss Henderson strikes her knuckles with a ruler. She is punished for questioning, not for a false accusation, and there is no collective blaming of the back row. Lorna Phillips does not escape a punishment; Hortense goes for her outside and Lorna runs off. The story then moves to England, where Hortense researches Black history and answers the Columbus question with evidence.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com analysis, which quotes 'What was Columbus doing here anyway?' and 'the sharp sting of the ruler'

findings.claim: "her dignity was never Miss Henderson's to remove, even if he tried".
findings.truth: Miss Henderson is a woman.
findings.evidence: internal

findings.claim: "published in 1984 in the collection Pack of Cards".
findings.truth: First published in 1984 in Corruption and Other Stories (Heinemann). Pack of Cards: Stories 1978-1986 is the 1986 collected volume that gathered it up.
findings.evidence: Heinemann 1984 contents listing for Corruption; Pack of Cards: Stories 1978-1986 (Heinemann, 1986)

findings.claim: "master the AQA Telling Tales 30-mark essay from."
findings.truth: The description ends mid-sentence.
findings.evidence: live field

findings.claim: "the Modern Texts question presents a single question on the Telling Tales anthology. The question will name a theme and ask how the anthology presents it." The six practice questions are all of the form 'How does the Telling Tales anthology present X?', and the exam tip tells students to pick the most relevant stories from across the anthology.
findings.truth: AQA offers a choice of two Telling Tales questions (Q15/Q16) and each names one story: 'How do writers present characters losing their innocence in "The Darkness Out There" and in one other story from Telling Tales?' The candidate writes about exactly two stories, one named by the board and one of their own choice.
findings.evidence: AQA specimen paper 8702/2 (filestore.aqa.org.uk/resources/english/AQA-87022-SQP.PDF), Section A Q15/Q16; same wording in June 2019, June 2020 and June 2023 papers

findings.claim: "the fragile grandmother-mother-son triangle" and "the grandmother-mother-son household" in Chemistry.
findings.truth: The grandmother is dead before the story opens. The household is grandfather, mother and son.
findings.evidence: story text and Lesson 1 of this unit

findings.claim: "In Chemistry, the grandfather's death is the event around which the story turns - he walks into the pond and drowns."
findings.truth: The grandfather drinks prussic acid from his chemistry shed. Lesson 1 of this same unit states this correctly, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com; revisionworld.com; Lesson 1

findings.claim: "the collection Learning to Swim".
findings.truth: The collection is Learning to Swim and Other Stories (1982). The short form is common and not misleading; left alone.
findings.evidence: publisher listings

findings.claim: The lesson makes 'deliberate ambiguity' the story's central AO2 feature and asks 'Is the father's motive ever confirmed?' Practice question 6 is built entirely on it.
findings.truth: Two defensible readings. The father never admits the plan to his son, so 'he never says it aloud' is fair; but the overheard conversation leaves the narrator in no doubt, and most study guides treat the motive as revealed rather than withheld. I softened the content and the two answer keys to 'he never admits it', and left practice question 6 standing. Recommendation: leave as it now reads; do not rebuild the question.
findings.evidence: apersonalanthology.com; shalom-education.com

findings.claim: "The narrator does not rage - she observes, remembers, and analyses"; "That the narrator retains her dignity throughout".
findings.truth: Hortense goes for Lorna Phillips outside the classroom and Lorna runs away, so the child does not stay composed. The claim can still be defended about the adult narrating voice. Recommendation: leave, since the tone claim is about the narration rather than the child's behaviour.
findings.evidence: shalom-education.com analysis

findings.claim: The glossary carries 'scapegoat', a term that appears nowhere in the lesson.
findings.truth: Harmless orphan entry; no student-facing error. Left alone.
findings.evidence: internal

findings.claim: None of the seven story lessons tells students that the exam question names one story and requires a second story of their choice.
findings.truth: Only Lesson 8 now carries the correct format. This is an omission rather than a false claim, so no edit was made in Lessons 1-7.
findings.evidence: AQA specimen 8702/2

summary: Every lesson carried at least one real error. The largest are three inverted plots: 'My Polish Teacher's Tie' is built on a non-recognition scene that does not happen, 'A Family Supper' has the father approving of a suicide he explicitly calls a mistake, and 'Invisible Mass of the Back Row' punishes the narrator for a false accusation rather than for questioning Columbus. Lesson 8 also misstates the AQA question format and kills Chemistry's grandfather by drowning.
